questions.questionMd: A student runs a Porter stemmer and observes that both **universe** and **university** produce the stem **univers**. This is an example of which failure mode?

options.text: Incorrect case folding applied before stemming
Over-stemming, which reduces retrieval precision
Under-stemming, which reduces retrieval recall
Accent folding, which merges morphologically unrelated forms

questions.explanationMd: Porter stemming has merged two semantically different words into the same stem. This is over-stemming and it can reduce precision by matching unrelated documents.

questions.questionMd: In a positional index, what specific information is stored for each term-document pair that is absent from a basic inverted index?

options.text: The term frequency of each token normalized by document length
The document frequency of the term across the entire corpus
The positions (offsets) of each token occurrence within the document
The byte offset of the document in the original corpus file

questions.explanationMd: A positional index stores the positions of each occurrence of a term within a document. These offsets make phrase and proximity queries possible.

questions.questionMd: Which of the following inputs causes whitespace tokenization to produce an incorrect or problematic result?

options.text: "search" treated as a single token
"nlp.stanford.edu" treated as a single token
"running" treated as a single token
"cat" treated as a single token

questions.explanationMd: Whitespace tokenization splits only on spaces, so a URL-like string such as `nlp.stanford.edu` remains one token even though punctuation may need special handling.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture, a biword index stores every consecutive pair of terms as a single index entry. What is the primary drawback of this approach compared to a positional index?

options.text: It cannot be combined with stopword removal because bigrams containing stopwords must be retained
It requires storing token positions for every document, making it 2-4 times larger than a basic inverted index
It is slower to build than a positional index because every bigram must be stemmed separately
Vocabulary size grows quadratically (from N terms to potentially N² bigrams), and it cannot support arbitrary phrase lengths

questions.explanationMd: A biword index can greatly increase vocabulary size because each adjacent pair becomes a term. It also directly supports only fixed two-word sequences, not arbitrary phrase lengths.

questions.questionMd: A developer uses `SELECT * FROM papers WHERE abstract LIKE '%heart attack%'` to find cardiology research. What is the most significant limitation of this approach compared to an IR system?

options.text: It returns no results for documents using the synonym "myocardial infarction".
It cannot filter results by publication date or author name
It is slower than an inverted index for corpora with fewer than one million rows
It requires a separate full-text parser before the SQL engine can execute

questions.explanationMd: A simple SQL `LIKE` query performs literal pattern matching and does not understand synonyms. An IR system can use analysis, expansion, or ranking to better handle vocabulary mismatch.

questions.questionMd: Which statement best captures the concept of TF saturation as modelled by BM25 and log-TF?

options.text: TF saturation means that once a term appears more than k1 times, it is completely ignored in scoring
Each additional occurrence of a term contributes progressively less to the relevance score
Each additional occurrence of a term contributes equally to the relevance score regardless of how many times it has already appeared
TF saturation increases the weight of the first occurrence of a term and sets all subsequent occurrences to zero

questions.explanationMd: TF saturation means term-frequency gains have diminishing returns. BM25 and log-TF avoid letting repeated occurrences increase the score linearly forever.

questions.questionMd: Compared to Porter stemming, WordNet lemmatization typically achieves a smaller percentage reduction in vocabulary size. Based on the lecture data, approximately what vocabulary reduction does lemmatization achieve versus Porter's ~29%?

options.text: Approximately 29%
Approximately 40%
Approximately 5%
Approximately 13%

questions.explanationMd: Lemmatization is usually less aggressive than Porter stemming, so it reduces vocabulary size by a smaller amount; the lecture figure is approximately 13%.

questions.questionMd: A new retrieval system retrieves a highly relevant document that was not included in the TREC judgment pool. How does this affect the system's measured evaluation score?

options.text: The evaluation is restarted with an expanded pool that includes the new system's results
The document is treated as irrelevant because it was never judged, which unfairly penalises the system
The document is excluded from the metric computation, leaving the system's score unchanged
The document receives the highest relevance grade automatically, rewarding novel retrieval

questions.explanationMd: In pooled evaluation, unjudged documents are commonly treated as nonrelevant for scoring. This can unfairly penalize systems that retrieve relevant documents outside the original pool.

questions.questionMd: Why can a leading wildcard query such as `*tion` not be resolved efficiently using only the standard forward-sorted dictionary?

options.text: A forward-sorted dictionary is compressed and cannot support random access required for suffix lookups
A forward-sorted dictionary provides no entry point for suffix patterns
The forward dictionary only indexes terms of more than three characters, excluding short suffix patterns
Leading wildcards require positional index data that is not stored in the dictionary layer

questions.explanationMd: A forward-sorted dictionary is efficient for prefixes, not suffixes. With a leading wildcard, the known characters are at the end, so there is no direct starting point for lookup.

questions.questionMd: In the Boolean retrieval model, what does a query return?

options.text: A probability distribution over matching documents
A set of document IDs with no ordering or relevance scores
A ranked list of documents sorted by relevance score
A set of document IDs sorted by term frequency

questions.explanationMd: The classic Boolean model returns documents that satisfy the Boolean expression. It does not rank them or assign relevance scores.

questions.questionMd: In the Vector Space Model (VSM), what determines the number of dimensions in a document vector?

options.text: The size of the vocabulary |V| of the entire collection
The number of documents in the collection
The number of tokens in the document being represented
The number of unique terms in the query

questions.explanationMd: In VSM, each vocabulary term corresponds to one dimension. Therefore the vector dimensionality is the collection vocabulary size `|V|`.

questions.questionMd: What is the recommended skip pointer interval for a postings list of length 400?
questions.explanationMd: A common heuristic is to place about `sqrt(P)` skip pointers for a postings list of length `P`. Since `sqrt(400)=20`, the recommended interval is 20.

questions.questionMd: In an OpenSearch cluster, which node type is responsible for receiving a client search request, routing it to the appropriate shards, and merging the results before returning them to the client?

options.text: The primary data node that holds the most shards.
The master node.
The coordinating node.
The replica node designated as the query leader for that request.

questions.explanationMd: The coordinating node receives the request, fans it out to relevant shards, gathers shard responses, and merges the results for the client.

questions.questionMd: A spelling corrector using a Jaccard threshold of 0.2 consistently returns no candidates for misspelled words of four characters or fewer. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The k-gram index only indexes vocabulary terms of five characters or more by default
Edit distance computation fails on short strings because the dynamic programming table is too small
Short words produce very few k-grams, so Jaccard scores are inherently lower
Short words are automatically classified as stop words and excluded from the k-gram index

questions.explanationMd: Short strings produce very few k-grams. A small difference can therefore reduce the Jaccard score sharply, causing candidates to fall below the threshold.

questions.questionMd: What must a developer do in code when computing NDCG@k for a query that has no relevant documents in the collection?

options.text: Assign each retrieved document a relevance grade of 1 and recompute normally
Exclude that query from the evaluation and reduce Q by 1 in the MAP formula
Return 1.0, because a system cannot be penalised for a query with no correct answers
Return 0.0 as a special-case guard, because IDCG=0 makes the formula undefined

questions.explanationMd: NDCG divides DCG by IDCG. If a query has no relevant documents, IDCG is zero, so the implementation needs a special-case guard to avoid division by zero.

questions.questionMd: A term is best defined as which of the following in the context of information retrieval indexing?

options.text: Any single occurrence of a word anywhere in a document collection
A normalized type that survives all preprocessing steps and enters the inverted index
A unique word form in the vocabulary before any normalization is applied
A token produced by splitting raw text on whitespace boundaries

questions.explanationMd: A term is the normalized representation that is actually indexed after tokenization and preprocessing such as lowercasing, stopword removal, or stemming.

questions.questionMd: An OpenSearch query uses `fields: ["title^3", "body^1"]` inside a `multi_match` clause. What does the `^3` notation mean for the `title` field?

options.text: OpenSearch searches the title field three times before falling back to the body field.
The query requires at least three matching terms in the title field before the document is considered a candidate.
The title field is indexed three times to increase recall for title matches.
A match in the title field contributes three times more to the relevance score than an equivalent match in the body field.

questions.explanationMd: The caret notation sets a field boost. `title^3` makes title matches contribute three times the weight of a field with boost 1, all else equal.

questions.questionMd: After L2 normalization is applied to all document vectors in the Vector Space Model, what geometric property do all normalized document vectors share?

options.text: All normalized document vectors have the same direction as the query vector for the collection's most common query
All normalized document vectors lie on the unit sphere, meaning their Euclidean norm equals 1
All normalized document vectors are projected onto a two-dimensional plane to enable fast ranking
All normalized document vectors become orthogonal to one another, eliminating redundant documents

questions.explanationMd: L2 normalization divides a vector by its Euclidean norm, so each normalized vector has length 1 and lies on the unit sphere.

questions.questionMd: Why is leading a query with a NOT operation alone considered poor practice?

options.text: It produces the same result as an AND query but takes longer to parse
It requires building a secondary inverted index from scratch at query time
It can only be applied after an OR merge has been completed
It requires scanning the entire corpus to find all document IDs not in the negated list

questions.explanationMd: A leading `NOT` defines the complement of a postings list. To compute it, the system may need to consider the full universe of document IDs.

questions.questionMd: Using VB encoding, a gap value of 5 requires how many bytes, and a gap value of 200 requires how many bytes?

options.text: 2 bytes for gap 5 and 2 bytes for gap 200
1 byte for gap 5 and 1 byte for gap 200
1 byte for gap 5 and 2 bytes for gap 200
2 bytes for gap 5 and 4 bytes for gap 200

questions.explanationMd: Variable-byte encoding stores values below 128 in one byte. A value such as 200 requires two bytes.

questions.questionMd: Which organisation established TREC (Text REtrieval Conference) in 1992 to provide shared benchmarks for IR evaluation?

options.text: IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers)
ACM (Association for Computing Machinery)
DARPA (Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency)
NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology)

questions.explanationMd: TREC was established by NIST to support shared evaluation tasks, test collections, and relevance judgments for information retrieval research.

questions.questionMd: What simplifying assumption does the Binary Independence Model (BIM) make about query terms when estimating the probability that a document is relevant?

options.text: Terms are assumed to appear the same number of times in every relevant document in the collection
Terms are assumed to be ranked by their IDF value before any probability estimation is performed
Terms are assumed to be statistically independent of one another given the relevance status of the document
Terms are assumed to have equal document frequency across the entire collection

questions.explanationMd: BIM assumes binary term occurrence and conditional independence of terms given relevance or nonrelevance. This simplifies probability estimation.

questions.questionMd: Which specific problem motivated the development of the BM25F variant?

options.text: Standard BM25 cannot handle multi-word queries because it sums scores term by term, a limitation BM25F overcomes
Standard BM25 produces negative IDF values for terms with very high document frequency, which BM25F corrects
Standard BM25 treats a document as a single flat text field
Standard BM25 requires all documents in the collection to have the same length, which BM25F relaxes with per-document normalization

questions.explanationMd: BM25F extends BM25 to handle structured documents with multiple fields, such as title, body, and anchor text, instead of treating everything as one flat field.

questions.questionMd: Which of the following correctly describes the relationship between a token, a type, and a term?

options.text: A term is one occurrence in text; a token is a unique normalized form; a type is what enters the index
A token is one occurrence in text; a type is a unique word form; a term is a normalized type entering the index
A type is one occurrence in text; a token is a unique word form; a term is produced by tokenization
A token and a type are interchangeable; a term is produced only after stopword removal

questions.explanationMd: A token is an occurrence in text, a type is a unique word form, and a term is the normalized form that is used in the index.

questions.questionMd: After applying the full preprocessing pipeline (tokenize -> lowercase -> stopword removal -> Porter stemming) to the input **The astronauts ORBITING the International Space Station**, which term in the output best illustrates a known over-stemming problem?

options.text: "station" produced from "Station"
"space" produced from "Space"
"intern" produced from "International"
"astronaut" produced from "astronauts"

questions.explanationMd: Porter stemming can reduce `international` to `intern`, which may merge unrelated meanings. That is a typical over-stemming issue.

questions.questionMd: Given the ranked list **R, I, I, R, R** (`R = relevant`, `I = irrelevant`), what is the Average Precision (AP)?
questions.explanationMd: Relevant documents occur at ranks 1, 4, and 5. AP is `(P@1 + P@4 + P@5)/3 = (1 + 0.5 + 0.6)/3 = 0.700`.

questions.questionMd: In Discounted Cumulative Gain (DCG), relevance scores are divided by the log base-2 of `(rank + 1)`. What user behavior does this logarithmic discount model?

options.text: Users read results in random order, so position should have no effect on contribution
Users prefer documents that are only marginally relevant at high ranks over highly relevant documents at low ranks
User attention diminishes at lower ranks, so a relevant document at rank 10 is worth less than one at rank 1
The discount penalizes systems that retrieve more than k documents, keeping result sets short

questions.explanationMd: DCG discounts gains at lower ranks because users are less likely to inspect or value results far down the ranked list.

questions.questionMd: The Probability Ranking Principle (PRP), which motivates BM25, states that documents should be ranked according to which criterion?

options.text: Decreasing probability of relevance given the document and query
Decreasing term frequency summed across all query terms
Increasing document frequency of the query terms in the collection
Decreasing document length relative to the collection average

questions.explanationMd: PRP says documents should be ordered by decreasing probability of relevance for the given query. BM25 is motivated by this probabilistic ranking view.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture, which scenario represents a case where stopword removal should NOT be applied?

options.text: A phrase query such as "to be or not to be"
Preprocessing queries submitted to a web-scale search engine
Indexing a large corpus of general news articles
A keyword query for a common technical term like "network"

questions.explanationMd: Stopwords may be essential in phrase queries. Removing words from `to be or not to be` would destroy the phrase structure and meaning.

questions.questionMd: As the raw term frequency `tf` in a document increases toward infinity, what value does the BM25 TF saturation function `tf * (k1 + 1) / (tf + k1)` approach?

options.text: The value `k1 + 1`, which is the asymptotic maximum that the saturation function never exceeds
The value 1, because the saturation function is normalized to the range [0, 1]
The value `k1`, which acts as a hard ceiling on TF contributions
The value `tf`, meaning the saturation function converges back to raw TF at very high counts

questions.explanationMd: For very large `tf`, the dominant terms are `tf*(k1+1)` in the numerator and `tf` in the denominator, so the expression approaches `k1+1`.

questions.questionMd: The NLTK English stopword list contains approximately how many words, and what is the approximate size of Lucene's default stopword list?

options.text: 500 words in NLTK and approximately 100 in Lucene
179 words in NLTK and approximately 179 in Lucene
179 words in NLTK and approximately 33 in Lucene
33 words in NLTK and approximately 179 in Lucene

questions.explanationMd: The lecture compares NLTK's larger English stopword list at about 179 words with Lucene's smaller default list at about 33 words.

questions.questionMd: An OpenSearch query uses `{ "fuzzy": { "title": { "value": "shudtle", "fuzziness": "AUTO" } } }`. Which concept from earlier in the course does this query clause directly implement at the search engine level?

options.text: Phonetic similarity hashing, which maps words that sound alike to the same hash bucket for retrieval.
Wildcard pattern expansion, which generates all terms matching a prefix or suffix pattern before scoring.
Edit distance (Levenshtein distance) based spelling correction.
Porter stemming, which normalizes inflected word forms to a common root before index lookup.

questions.explanationMd: OpenSearch fuzzy matching uses edit-distance style matching, commonly Levenshtein distance, to find terms close to the misspelled query term.

questions.questionMd: In OpenSearch's text analysis pipeline, what is the correct order of processing stages?

options.text: Tokenizer -> Character filters -> Token filters
Token filters -> Tokenizer -> Character filters
Character filters -> Tokenizer -> Token filters

questions.explanationMd: Character filters clean or transform the raw text before tokenization. The tokenizer then creates tokens, and token filters modify those tokens.

questions.questionMd: Which sequence correctly describes the three-stage spelling correction pipeline?

options.text: Jaccard similarity filtering -> k-gram candidate retrieval -> edit distance ranking
Edit distance ranking -> Jaccard similarity filtering -> k-gram candidate retrieval
K-gram candidate retrieval -> edit distance ranking -> Jaccard similarity filtering
K-gram candidate retrieval -> Jaccard similarity filtering -> edit distance ranking

questions.explanationMd: The usual pipeline first retrieves candidates using k-grams, filters them with Jaccard similarity, and then ranks the remaining candidates by edit distance.

questions.questionMd: A colleague argues that MAP is always preferable to NDCG@k because MAP considers the entire ranked list rather than a cutoff. Which counter-argument best explains a key limitation of MAP?

options.text: MAP penalises systems that retrieve more than k documents, making deep retrieval unfair
MAP is only defined for navigational queries where exactly one relevant document exists
MAP requires a larger query set than NDCG@k to produce stable estimates
MAP assumes binary relevance

questions.explanationMd: MAP is based on binary relevance judgments. NDCG can naturally use graded relevance, so it can distinguish highly relevant from partially relevant documents.

questions.questionMd: Why is cosine similarity preferred over the raw dot product for ranking documents in the Vector Space Model?

options.text: Cosine similarity is faster to compute than the dot product for large sparse vectors
Cosine similarity produces scores in the range [-1, 1] while dot products are unbounded
Cosine similarity normalizes for document length, preventing longer documents from automatically scoring higher than shorter, more focused ones
Cosine similarity accounts for term order, while the dot product does not

questions.explanationMd: The raw dot product can favor longer documents with larger vector magnitudes. Cosine similarity compares vector direction by normalizing vector lengths.

questions.questionMd: Given two k-gram sets A and B, which expression correctly computes their Jaccard similarity?
questions.explanationMd: Jaccard similarity is the size of the intersection divided by the size of the union of the two sets.

questions.questionMd: Why does the Vector Space Model use cosine similarity rather than Euclidean distance to compare document and query vectors?

options.text: Euclidean distance produces values outside the range [0, 1], making it impossible to rank documents consistently
Euclidean distance would make a long document seem very different from a short one covering the same topics
Euclidean distance cannot be computed for high-dimensional vectors, whereas cosine similarity is defined for any number of dimensions
Cosine similarity is always faster to compute than Euclidean distance for sparse TF-IDF vectors

questions.explanationMd: Euclidean distance is sensitive to vector magnitude. A long and a short document about the same topic may be far apart by distance even if their term distributions are similar.

questions.questionMd: A term has high TF in a document but very low IDF across the collection. What does this combination indicate about the term's usefulness as a relevance signal?

options.text: The term is a weak discriminator because it appears frequently in many documents
The term should be removed from the index because its combined TF-IDF weight will be exactly zero
The term is highly informative because low IDF indicates it appears in very few documents
The term is a strong relevance signal because high TF always dominates the combined TF-IDF weight

questions.explanationMd: Low IDF means the term appears in many documents, so it is not very discriminative even if it appears often in one document.

questions.questionMd: In the Boolean retrieval model, which operator precedence order is correct when no parentheses are used?

options.text: AND is evaluated first, then NOT, then OR
NOT is evaluated first, then AND, then OR
NOT and AND share equal precedence and are evaluated before OR
OR is evaluated first, then AND, then NOT

questions.explanationMd: The standard precedence order is `NOT` first, then `AND`, then `OR`, unless parentheses override it.

questions.questionMd: What retrieval behavior results when the BM25 parameter `k1` is set to 0?

options.text: The BM25 score becomes equivalent to raw TF multiplied by IDF with no saturation
Length normalization is disabled because the denominator reduces to the raw term frequency
The IDF component dominates entirely and term frequency is weighted at its maximum possible value
The TF component becomes binary - only whether a term is present matters, not how many times it appears

questions.explanationMd: With `k1 = 0`, the BM25 TF factor becomes 1 for any present term. Thus frequency no longer matters beyond presence or absence.

questions.questionMd: What is the typical relationship between Precision and Recall as more documents are retrieved?

options.text: Precision tends to decrease as Recall increases, reflecting a fundamental tradeoff
Both Precision and Recall increase together as more documents are retrieved
Precision stays constant while Recall increases
Recall decreases as Precision increases, because early ranks contain the best results

questions.explanationMd: Retrieving more documents usually finds more relevant documents, increasing recall, but also adds more nonrelevant documents, which tends to lower precision.

questions.questionMd: Which statement correctly describes a key theoretical difference between BM25 and TF-IDF with cosine similarity?

options.text: Both BM25 and TF-IDF are derived from the Binary Independence Model but differ only in their length normalization
BM25 is a purely heuristic method, while TF-IDF has a formal probabilistic derivation from the Robertson-Spärck Jones weight
BM25 is derived from the Binary Independence Model and the Probability Ranking Principle, while TF-IDF is a heuristic weighting scheme
TF-IDF is derived from the Probability Ranking Principle, while BM25 is an empirical approximation with no theoretical basis

questions.explanationMd: BM25 has a probabilistic motivation through BIM and PRP. TF-IDF with cosine similarity is a strong heuristic weighting and vector-space approach.

questions.questionMd: When optimizing a multi-term AND query by sorting operands in order of ascending document frequency, what is the primary benefit?

options.text: The total number of postings lists loaded into memory is reduced
Intermediate result sets shrink fastest when processing begins with the rarest terms
Skip pointers become unnecessary for the remaining operations
The OR merge step is eliminated from the query plan

questions.explanationMd: For an AND query, starting with the rarest terms produces smaller intermediate intersections early, reducing later comparison work.

questions.questionMd: What is the core intuition behind Inverse Document Frequency (IDF) as used in TF-IDF weighting?

options.text: Terms that appear in many documents carry little discriminating information and should receive lower weights
IDF increases the weight of terms that co-occur with stopwords
IDF penalizes terms based on how frequently they appear within a single document
Terms that appear in many documents are more likely to be relevant to any query

questions.explanationMd: IDF gives lower weight to terms that appear in many documents because common terms are less useful for distinguishing relevant documents.

questions.questionMd: Which of the following is a key advantage of the Snowball stemmer over the original Porter stemmer?

options.text: Snowball always produces real dictionary words as output, unlike Porter
Snowball provides multilingual support for languages
Snowball applies more aggressive suffix stripping, achieving a smaller vocabulary
Snowball uses a morphological lexicon instead of rule-based suffix removal

questions.explanationMd: Snowball generalizes stemming algorithms and provides support for multiple languages, while the original Porter stemmer is focused on English.

questions.questionMd: In the Average Precision formula `AP = (1/R) x Σ P@k`, what does the summation run over?

options.text: The top-k positions specified by the evaluation cutoff
All rank positions from 1 to the total number of retrieved documents
Only the rank positions k where the retrieved document is relevant
All positions where the retrieved document is irrelevant, as a penalty term

questions.explanationMd: Average Precision averages precision values only at ranks where a relevant document is retrieved.

questions.questionMd: In SMART notation, what does the scheme `lnc` specify for document weighting?

options.text: Logarithmic TF, natural IDF, cosine normalization
Log-average TF, natural IDF, no normalization
Logarithmic TF, no IDF, cosine normalization
Natural TF, no IDF, cosine normalization

questions.explanationMd: In SMART notation, `l` means logarithmic TF, `n` means no IDF, and `c` means cosine normalization.

questions.questionMd: In the IR triangle model, which concept sits at the centre connecting the query, the document, and the information need?

options.text: Vocabulary
Ranking
Precision
Relevance

questions.explanationMd: Relevance connects the user's information need, the query representation, and the documents returned by the system.

questions.questionMd: Which formula correctly defines Precision in an information retrieval evaluation context?

options.text: |Relevant ∩ Retrieved| / |Retrieved|
|Relevant| / (|Relevant| + |Retrieved|)
|Retrieved| / |Relevant|
|Relevant ∩ Retrieved| / |Relevant|

questions.explanationMd: Precision measures the fraction of retrieved documents that are relevant: relevant retrieved documents divided by all retrieved documents.

questions.questionMd: A student searches for **flight delays snow**. Their actual need is to understand why winter weather disrupts air travel. What does this example best illustrate?

options.text: Queries and information needs are equivalent when the user is precise
A query is always a lossy compression of the underlying information need
Search engines require queries to match document text exactly
Information needs can be fully captured in two or three words

questions.explanationMd: A short query is only an imperfect expression of a broader information need. It often omits context, intent, and desired explanation.

questions.questionMd: Which of the following operations in OpenSearch relies on DocValues rather than the inverted index?

options.text: Storing the original human-readable content of a document so it can be displayed in search results.
Finding all documents that contain the term "laptop" in a full-text search query.
Applying a Porter stemmer to tokenize and normalize query terms at search time.
Sorting results by a numeric price field and computing aggregation buckets for faceted navigation.

questions.explanationMd: DocValues are column-oriented on-disk structures used for sorting, aggregations, and faceting. Full-text search relies mainly on the inverted index.

questions.questionMd: After intersecting k-gram postings to resolve a wildcard query, why is a mandatory post-filtering step required?

options.text: The k-gram intersection can only retrieve terms from a single partition of the vocabulary at a time
K-gram matching is a necessary but not sufficient condition
K-gram postings lists are unsorted, so the intersection result contains duplicate terms
Post-filtering converts k-gram integer IDs back into human-readable vocabulary terms

questions.explanationMd: Terms sharing the required k-grams may still fail the original wildcard pattern. Post-filtering checks the actual wildcard expression.

questions.questionMd: A developer wants to build a faceted navigation sidebar that counts how many products belong to each category (e.g., **Electronics: 120**, **Clothing: 85**). Which field type should the category field use in the OpenSearch mapping?

options.text: text, because it supports full-text analysis which enables partial matching of category names.
keyword, because it stores exact unanalyzed values that can be used in terms aggregations.
integer, because aggregation requires numeric fields to produce accurate bucket counts.
text with the english analyzer, so that category names are stemmed before aggregation.

questions.explanationMd: A `keyword` field stores exact values and is appropriate for terms aggregations, faceting, and category counts.

questions.questionMd: Which 1960s development is credited as the first systematic, reproducible evaluation of IR systems, establishing the methodology of using test collections and relevance judgments?

options.text: The SMART system developed by Salton at Cornell
The launch of MEDLARS at the National Library of Medicine
The Cranfield experiments
The introduction of Luhn's automatic keyword extraction

questions.explanationMd: The Cranfield experiments established the test-collection methodology with queries, documents, and relevance judgments for reproducible IR evaluation.

questions.questionMd: Heap's Law describes how vocabulary size V grows with the total number of tokens N in a corpus. Which statement correctly characterizes this growth?

options.text: Vocabulary grows sub-linearly and never fully stops growing
Vocabulary grows linearly, adding a fixed number of new terms per document
Vocabulary growth stops once the corpus exceeds a threshold size
Vocabulary grows exponentially in proportion to the square of N

questions.explanationMd: Heap's Law models vocabulary growth as sub-linear in the number of tokens. New terms keep appearing, but at a decreasing rate.

questions.questionMd: The Soundex algorithm is best described as a tool designed for which specific purpose?

options.text: Wildcard query resolution by hashing vocabulary terms into fixed-length codes
General-purpose spelling correction for any English vocabulary term
Phonetic matching of proper names by encoding names that sound similar to the same code
Ranking spelling correction candidates by their edit distance from a misspelled query

questions.explanationMd: Soundex encodes names by approximate pronunciation so that similar-sounding names can be matched despite spelling differences.

questions.questionMd: A term has a document frequency (DF) of 500 and a term frequency (TF) of 12 in one particular document. What does the DF value of 500 indicate?

options.text: The term's postings list contains 500 position entries
The term appears in 500 different documents in the corpus
The term appears in documents with an average length of 500 tokens
The term appears 500 times across all documents combined

questions.explanationMd: Document frequency counts how many documents contain the term, not how many total times the term occurs.

questions.questionMd: In IR system design, Boolean retrieval and neural reranking sit at opposite ends of a fundamental tradeoff. Which pair of terms correctly names the two competing goals?

options.text: Index compression versus index coverage
Precision (result quality) versus recall (result completeness)
Efficiency (speed and scale) versus effectiveness (accuracy and relevance)
Offline processing versus online processing

questions.explanationMd: Boolean retrieval is often efficient and scalable, while neural reranking aims for stronger relevance effectiveness at higher computational cost.

questions.questionMd: Case folding converts **Apple** to **apple** during normalization. According to the lecture, which specific example demonstrates that lowercasing is NOT always a safe operation?

options.text: "Apple" (company name) vs. "apple" (the fruit) carry different meanings
"NASA" should always be lowercased to "nasa" for consistency
"Running" and "running" should always be treated as the same term
Accent folding should always be performed before case folding

questions.explanationMd: Lowercasing can remove meaningful distinctions. `Apple` as a company and `apple` as a fruit are different entities even though their lowercase forms match.
